claims.source: In this regard, despite predicted to be within the hydrophobic lipid bilayer, the negatively-charged amino acid D961 and polar amino acid T976 of EMC1 are highly conserved (Figure 4A), suggesting an important function.
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The polar amino acid T976 of EMC1 is highly conserved.
claims.source: In this regard, despite predicted to be within the hydrophobic lipid bilayer, the negatively-charged amino acid D961 and polar amino acid T976 of EMC1 are highly conserved (Figure 4A), suggesting an important function.
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: D961A and T976A EMC1 mutants display an ER localization pattern similar to WT EMC1.
claims.source: First, when transfected, these mutants displayed an ER localization pattern as the endogenous ER membrane protein BAP31, similar to transfected WT EMC1 (Figure 4B, compare second and third rows to the top row), indicating that D961A and T976A EMC1 are localized to the ER.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: D961A and T976A EMC1 mutants are properly oriented in the ER membrane.
claims.source: We found that both the D961A and T976A EMC1-FLAG mutants displayed a similar faster migration pattern as WT EMC1-FLAG when treated with this deglycosidase (Figure 4C, compare odd to even lanes), suggesting that the orientation of the EMC1 mutants is the same as WT EMC1.
claims.evidence: Supported by deglycosylation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: D961A and T976A EMC1 mutants can bind to C18.
claims.source: Third, we interrogated whether the EMC1 mutants can bind to EMC1's newly identified binding partner C18, and found that they did (Figure 4D, top panel, compare lane 2 to lanes 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Adding back WT EMC1 to EMC1-depleted cells fully rescues SV40 infection.
claims.source: Using this protocol, we found that adding back WT EMC1 to cells transfected with EMC1 siRNA #1 fully rescued SV40 infection (Figure 4E, compare third to second bar), unambiguously demonstrating that the block in SV40 infection and ER-to-cytosol transport due to EMC1 siRNA #1 treatment is specifically a result of depleting EMC1 and not to off-target effects.
claims.evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Expressing T976A EMC1 mutant restores SV40 infection in EMC1-depleted cells.
claims.source: Importantly, whereas expressing the T976A mutant also restored infection, expression of the D961A mutant did not (Figure 4E, compare fifth to fourth bars).
claims.evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Expressing D961A EMC1 mutant does not restore SV40 infection in EMC1-depleted cells.
claims.source: Importantly, whereas expressing the T976A mutant also restored infection, expression of the D961A mutant did not (Figure 4E, compare fifth to fourth bars).
claims.evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: D961A EMC1 mutant binds to EMC3 transmembrane protein similar to WT EMC1.
claims.source: It is unlikely that the D961A mutant failed to form a complex with the EMC because it binds to the EMC3 transmembrane protein, similar to WT EMC1 (Figure 4F, top panel, compare lane 3 to 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The D961 residue of EMC1 plays a specific and crucial role during SV40 infection.
claims.source: These findings thus strongly suggest that the D961 residue of EMC1 plays a specific and crucial role during SV40 infection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knockdown-rescue experiments.

claims.claim: EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG truncation variant does not restore SV40 infection in EMC1-depleted cells.
claims.source: We next asked if a FLAG-tagged EMC1 truncation variant that harbors the luminal domain and including residues up to D961 [EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG] is functional. We found that it was not because expressing this construct in EMC1 knocked down cells did not restore SV40 infection (Figure 4G), even though this construct displayed an ER expression pattern (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: Supported by knockdown-rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: An intact EMC1 membrane-spanning domain is required to promote SV40 ER membrane transport.
claims.source: These findings indicate that an intact EMC1 membrane-spanning domain, presumably including residue D961, is required to promote SV40 ER membrane transport.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the truncation mutant experiments.

claims.claim: SV40 crosses the ER membrane to reach the cytosol approximately 7–8 hours post infection.
claims.source: We previously established that SV40 crosses the ER membrane to reach the cytosol approximately 7–8 hpi (Inoue and Tsai, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: EMC1 binds to SV40 at 7 hours post infection but not at 2 or 15 hours post infection.
claims.source: In a time-course experiment, we found that in cells expressing WT EMC1-FLAG, precipitating EMC1 pulled down SV40 only at 7 but not 2 or 15 hpi (Figure 5A, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1 and 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation time-course data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: EMC1 binds to SV40 at approximately the time point when the virus is expected to penetrate the ER membrane.
claims.source: Thus EMC1 binds to SV40 at approximately the time point when the virus is expected to penetrate the ER membrane; this interaction is lost later in the course of infection, perhaps reflecting a completion of SV40 cytosol arrival.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the time-course binding data.

claims.claim: D961A EMC1 mutant does not efficiently bind to SV40 compared to WT EMC1.
claims.source: To test if D961 of EMC1 mediates the EMC1-SV40 interaction, we found that the D961A EMC1-FLAG mutant did not efficiently precipitate the virus when compared to WT EMC1-FLAG (Figure 5B, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1; the virus binding level is quantified in the bottom bar graph), suggesting that EMC1's D961 residue is critical in supporting virus binding.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: SV40 co-precipitates poorly with truncated EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG construct compared to WT EMC1-FLAG during infection.
claims.source: Additionally, as SV40 co-precipitates poorly with the truncated EMC1 (1-961)-FLAG construct when compared to WT EMC1-FLAG during infection (Figure 5C, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1; quantified in the bottom bar graph), the D961 residue must nonetheless act in the context of the rest of EMC1's transmembrane domain to fully support virus interaction.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: SV40's association with WT EMC1 is sensitive to high salt wash.
claims.source: SV40's association with WT EMC1 is sensitive to high salt (0.5 M NaCl) wash (Figure 5D, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), in line with the idea that this binding event is mediated by an electrostatic interaction.
claims.evidence: Supported by high salt wash experiment data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The EMC1-SV40 binding event is mediated by an electrostatic interaction.
claims.source: SV40's association with WT EMC1 is sensitive to high salt (0.5 M NaCl) wash (Figure 5D, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), in line with the idea that this binding event is mediated by an electrostatic interaction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the salt sensitivity of the interaction.

claims.claim: There is a strong correlation between EMC1's ability to interact with SV40 and promote infection.
claims.source: These results establish a strong correlation between EMC1's ability to interact with the virus and promote infection, as the D961 residue is crucial to both processes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: Purified WT and D961A EMC1 samples do not contain other EMC subunits.
claims.source: Mass spectrometry analyses of the WT and D961A EMC1 samples indicated that no other EMC subunits were present (not shown).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis.

claims.claim: SV40 is partially destabilized in the ER.
claims.source: Previous studies revealed that SV40 is partially destabilized in the ER (Inoue et al., 2015; Magnuson et al., 2005; Walczak and Tsai, 2011; Nelson et al., 2012), an effect that can be mimicked in part by treating purified SV40 with DTT (which reduces the SV40 disulfide bonds) and EGTA (which removes calcium bound to the virus).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Treating purified SV40 with DTT and EGTA mimics ER-induced conformational changes.
claims.source: Previous studies revealed that SV40 is partially destabilized in the ER (Inoue et al., 2015; Magnuson et al., 2005; Walczak and Tsai, 2011; Nelson et al., 2012), an effect that can be mimicked in part by treating purified SV40 with DTT (which reduces the SV40 disulfide bonds) and EGTA (which removes calcium bound to the virus).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies and the known effects of DTT and EGTA.

claims.claim: EMC1 directly interacts with DTT/EGTA-treated SV40 but not untreated native SV40.
claims.source: Indeed, when SV40 was incubated with either GFP-FLAG or WT EMC1-FLAG in the presence or absence of DTT/EGTA, pull down of EMC1 but not GFP precipitated SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), demonstrating a direct EMC1-SV40 interaction. By contrast, EMC1 did not interact with untreated native SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, lanes 3 and 4), suggesting that EMC1 recognizes a partially destabilized form of SV40.
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: EMC1 recognizes a partially destabilized form of SV40.
claims.source: Indeed, when SV40 was incubated with either GFP-FLAG or WT EMC1-FLAG in the presence or absence of DTT/EGTA, pull down of EMC1 but not GFP precipitated SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1), demonstrating a direct EMC1-SV40 interaction. By contrast, EMC1 did not interact with untreated native SV40 (Figure 5F, top panel, lanes 3 and 4), suggesting that EMC1 recognizes a partially destabilized form of SV40.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential binding to treated vs untreated virus.

claims.claim: D961A EMC1 mutant binds to DTT-EGTA destabilized SV40 less efficiently than WT EMC1 in vitro.
claims.source: Moreover, using this in vitro approach, we found that the D961A EMC1 mutant binds to DTT-EGTA destabilized SV40 much less efficiently than WT EMC1 (Figure 5G, top panel, compare lane 1 to 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: EMC1 binds to VP1, but VP2 and VP3 also play important roles in supporting the EMC1-SV40 interaction.
claims.source: To determine the viral components interacting with EMC1, we used VP1-containing viral-like-particles (VP1-VLP) devoid of VP2 and VP3 (Figure 5H, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1). Our results demonstrated that precipitating WT EMC1-FLAG pulled down less VP1-VLP when compared to WT SV40 (Figure 5H, top panel, compare lane 4 to 3; quantified in the right graph). These findings indicate that, although EMC1 binds to VP1, the internal proteins VP2 and VP3 also play important roles in supporting this interaction.
claims.evidence: Supported by VP1-VLP binding assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Depleting EMC1 causes a portion of ER-localized SV40 to disassemble prematurely.
claims.source: When ER-localized virus derived from control cells was analyzed, the virus was found in the bottom fraction (Figure 6A, top panel), suggesting that SV40 remains largely intact despite being partially destabilized in the ER. However, when ER-localized virus derived from EMC1-depleted cells was isolated and subjected to the same procedure, a distinct virus pool is present throughout the higher fractions corresponding to disassembled virus (Figure 6A, 2nd panel); these species likely reflect single, as well as oligomeric, VP1 pentamers. Hence a portion of ER-localized SV40 disassembles prematurely in EMC1-depleted cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: EMC1 acts to stabilize SV40.
claims.source: As disassembled ER-localized virus is found in the absence of EMC1, this finding suggests that EMC1 acts to stabilize SV40.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the disassembly assay results.

claims.claim: Depleting SGTA or C18 does not cause premature SV40 disassembly.
claims.source: To rule out the possibility that simply imposing a block in SV40 ER-to-cytosol transport is sufficient to cause viral premature disassembly, ER-localized virus derived from SGTA- or C18-depleted cells, which also display a strong impairment in SV40 ER-to-cytosol transport (Walczak et al., 2014; Goodwin et al., 2011), was isolated and subjected to the same procedure. However, no disassembled virus appeared in these samples (Figure 6A, 3rd and 4th panels).
claims.evidence: Supported by sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The appearance of disassembled virus is not a general consequence of blocking ER membrane transport.
claims.source: Thus, the appearance of the disassembled virus is not a general consequence of blocking ER membrane transport, but points to a specific role of EMC1 in conferring virus stability.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing EMC1 depletion to SGTA/C18 depletion.

claims.claim: ER-localized SV40 from EMC1-depleted cells is more sensitive to proteolytic digestion by trypsin than virus from control cells.
claims.source: We used a limited proteolysis approach as an independent strategy to further assess SV40's conformational state when EMC1 is depleted – this is a sensitive method used to detect subtle structural changes that may not be readily revealed by the sucrose gradient sedimentation assay. Using this approach, we found that ER-localized SV40 derived from EMC1-depleted cells is more sensitive to proteolytic digestion by trypsin than virus derived from control cells (Figure 6B, compare bottom to top panels).
claims.evidence: Supported by limited proteolysis assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: SV40 is structurally exposed when EMC1 is absent.
claims.source: These findings indicate that SV40 is structurally exposed when EMC1 is absent, supporting the sucrose sedimentation data demonstrating that the viral particle experiences premature disassembly without EMC1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proteolysis assay results.

claims.claim: EMC1 protects SV40 against DTT/EGTA-induced disassembly in vitro.
claims.source: However, if EMC1 was simultaneously incubated in the presence of the destabilizing agents (DTT/EGTA), a significant pool of SV40 sediments to the bottom fraction, representing intact virus (Figure 6C, third panel). This finding suggests that EMC1 protects SV40 against disassembly, supporting the notion that it acts to stabilize the virus.
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: WT EMC1 cannot confer protection against viral disassembly once the virus has disassembled.
claims.source: However, when SV40 was pre-treated with DTT/EGTA and then incubated with WT EMC1, the virus level that sediments to the bottom fraction decreased significantly compared to when WT EMC1 was simultaneously incubated with DTT/EGTA (Figure 6C, compare fourth to third panel). This result demonstrates that WT EMC1 cannot confer protection against viral disassembly once the virus has disassembled.
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: D961A EMC1 mutant does not provide strong protection against DTT/EGTA-induced SV40 disassembly compared to WT EMC1.
claims.source: Importantly, the D961A EMC1 mutant did not provide strong protection against DTT/EGTA-induced SV40 disassembly when compared to WT EMC1 (Figure 6C, compare fifth to third panel).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: WT EMC1 protected more than 66% of SV40 against DTT/EGTA-triggered disassembly whereas D961A mutant protected approximately 18%.
claims.source: When quantified, WT EMC1 protected more than 66% of SV40 against DTT/EGTA-triggered disassembly whereas the mutant EMC1 protected approximately 18% of the virus against disassembly, where virus in fractions 1–6 represents disassembled virus and those in fractions 7–9 represents largely intact particles (Ravindran et al., 2015) (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification of in vitro sucrose sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Cell-based results coupled with in vitro reconstitution experiments strongly argue that EMC1 imparts a stabilizing force to SV40 during ER membrane penetration.
claims.source: Hence our cell-based results coupled with the in vitro reconstitution experiments strongly argue that EMC1 imparts a stabilizing force to the virus during the ER membrane penetration process.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches.

claims.claim: Hsc70 cannot capture SV40 when EMC1 is downregulated.
claims.source: We reasoned that a prematurely disassembled virus might not assume the proper conformation to properly engage the Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 machinery that normally extracts SV40 into the cytosol - this would explain why EMC1 depletion blocks cytosol entry of the virus. To test this possibility, we first asked if Hsc70 is able to capture SV40 when EMC1 is downregulated. Cells expressing S-tagged Hsc70 (Hsc70-S) were transfected with either scrambled or EMC1 #1 siRNA. When Hsc70-S was affinity purified from the resulting WCE, SV40 was only pulled down using extracts from control but not EMC1-depleted cells (Figure 7A, top panel, compare lane 2 to 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Knocking down EMC1 does not affect the integrity of the Hsc70-SGTA interaction.
claims.source: By contrast, endogenous SGTA was precipitated under both conditions (Figure 7A, second panel, compare lane 1 to 2), suggesting that knocking down EMC1 did not affect the integrity of the Hsc70-SGTA interaction.
claims.evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: EMC1 knockdown prevents SGTA from binding to SV40.
claims.source: A similar result was found for SGTA: EMC1 knockdown prevents (transfected) SGTA from binding to SV40 (Figure 7A, top panel, compare lane 4 to 3), but not to endogenous Hsc70 (Figure 7A, second panel, compare lane 4 to 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: EMC1 is required to allow SV40 to engage the cytosolic extraction machinery.
claims.source: Together, these findings demonstrate that EMC1 is required to allow SV40 to engage the cytosolic extraction machinery.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding experiments with Hsc70 and SGTA.

claims.claim: The extraction machinery remains tethered to ER membrane J-proteins even in EMC1's absence.
claims.source: However, we found that precipitating C18-S pulled down endogenous Hsc70 and SGTA regardless of EMC1's presence (Figure 7B, top and second panels, compare lane 2 to 1); silencing EMC1 also preserved the interaction between SGTA and Hsp105 with another J-protein B14 (not shown). Hence, as the extraction machinery remains tethered to ER membrane J-proteins even in EMC1's absence, the simplest explanation for why depleting EMC1 prevents the extraction machinery from capturing SV40 is that the viral particle experienced premature disassembly, thereby precluding its interaction with this machinery.
claims.evidence: Supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The simplest explanation for why depleting EMC1 prevents the extraction machinery from capturing SV40 is that the viral particle experienced premature disassembly.
claims.source: Hence, as the extraction machinery remains tethered to ER membrane J-proteins even in EMC1's absence, the simplest explanation for why depleting EMC1 prevents the extraction machinery from capturing SV40 is that the viral particle experienced premature disassembly, thereby precluding its interaction with this machinery.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing extraction machinery localization is preserved but virus binding is lost.

claims.claim: Virus stabilization can serve a crucial function during viral entry.
claims.source: Host-encoded forces stabilizing a viral particle are generally exploited to support viral assembly (Prange et al., 1999; Cobbold et al., 2001). The resulting assembled virus in turn exits the host cell to cause the next round of infection. By contrast, we report here that virus stabilization can also serve a crucial function during viral entry.
claims.evidence: This is a novel conclusion drawn from the current study in contrast to previous knowledge.

claims.claim: EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone, deploying its D961 residue to engage membrane-embedded SV40 and promote ER membrane penetration.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that the largest component of the ER membrane complex EMC called EMC1 executes an essential role during SV40 ER-to-cytosol membrane transport, a decisive entry step for this non-enveloped virus. Our data strongly suggest that EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone, deploying its highly conserved D961 residue in order to engage the membrane-embedded SV40 and promote the ER membrane penetration event (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental data.

claims.claim: D961 residue likely functions within the membrane-spanning domain or at the membrane border.
claims.source: This residue likely functions within the membrane-spanning domain (or at the membrane border), and must act in concert with the rest of EMC1's transmembrane domain to accomplish its role.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural predictions and functional data.

claims.claim: EMC1's interaction stabilizes the overall SV40 architecture within the ER lipid bilayer or at the earliest phase of membrane insertion.
claims.source: Because membrane-penetrating SV40 is partially destabilized, EMC1's interaction stabilizes the overall viral architecture either within the ER lipid bilayer or at the earliest phase of the membrane insertion process.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Stabilization maintains SV40 in a transport-competent state, enabling recognition by the cytosolic Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 extraction machinery.
claims.source: Importantly, stabilization maintains the virus in a transport-competent state, enabling it to be recognized by the cytosolic Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 extraction machinery, which completes the membrane transport process by ejecting the virus into the cytosol.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing stabilization is required for extraction machinery engagement.

claims.claim: Coordinated interplay between destabilization and stabilization drives PyV entry.
claims.source: Thus, ironically, while host encoded forces that destabilize SV40 are known to promote viral ER-to-cytosol transport (Ravindran et al., 2015), an opposing force that stabilizes SV40 appears to play an equally important role during this step. The concept that coordinated interplay between destabilization and stabilization drive PyV entry may have broad implications in illuminating other viral entry mechanisms, including enveloped viruses.
claims.evidence: This is the main conceptual conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: Host factors stabilize the HIV viral capsid to prevent premature uncoating during entry.
claims.source: For instance, in destabilizing the enveloped virus HIV during entry, host factors also stabilize the viral capsid in a concerted manner in order to prevent its premature uncoating, which otherwise prevents infection (Guth and Sodroski, 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on HIV.

claims.claim: Coordinated destabilization-stabilization is an important concept during viral entry.
claims.source: Thus, there is clearly a precedent for the hypothesis that coordinated destabilization-stabilization is an important (yet poorly-explored) concept during viral entry.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current findings to HIV entry.

claims.claim: EMC1 recognizes positively-charged residues exposed in the membrane-inserted SV40.
claims.source: Our finding that EMC1's D961 residue is essential for binding to and stabilizing the partially destabilized SV40 suggests that EMC1 recognizes positively-charged residues exposed in the membrane-inserted virus.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the charge properties of D961 and the binding data.

claims.claim: EMC1's transmembrane domain might function as a 'sensor', recognizing exposure of aberrant membrane-spanning residues in substrates.
claims.source: Hence, EMC1's transmembrane domain might function as a 'sensor', recognizing exposure of aberrant membrane-spanning residues in substrates.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about EMC1's general mechanism of action.

claims.claim: VP2 and VP3 are exposed in the membrane-inserted virus.
claims.source: Because VP2 and VP3 are exposed in the membrane-inserted virus (Magnuson et al., 2005; Norkin et al., 2002; Rainey-Barger et al., 2007; Kuksin and Norkin, 2012; Daniels et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2011), it is tempting to speculate that despite the overall hydrophobic nature of these internal proteins, positively-charged residues of VP2/VP3 may be sensed by EMC1 via D961.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Positively-charged residues of VP2/VP3 may be sensed by EMC1 via D961.
claims.source: Because VP2 and VP3 are exposed in the membrane-inserted virus (Magnuson et al., 2005; Norkin et al., 2002; Rainey-Barger et al., 2007; Kuksin and Norkin, 2012; Daniels et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2011), it is tempting to speculate that despite the overall hydrophobic nature of these internal proteins, positively-charged residues of VP2/VP3 may be sensed by EMC1 via D961.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the VP2/VP3 exposure and the D961 charge.

claims.claim: A VP1-VLP lacking VP2 and VP3 displayed less efficient binding to EMC1 compared to WT SV40.
claims.source: This idea is supported by our data that a VP1-VLP lacking VP2 and VP3 displayed less efficient binding to EMC1 when compared to WT SV40 that harbors these internal proteins.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Positively-charged residues exposed in VP1 may also represent the contact point with EMC1.
claims.source: Positively-charged residues exposed in the coat protein VP1 may also represent the contact point with EMC1, since VP1-VLP appears to be sufficient in providing some level of interaction with this transmembrane protein.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the VP1-VLP binding data.

claims.claim: EMC1 stabilization might reflect a passive process of shielding exposed charges on SV40.
claims.source: The postulated exposure of the positively-charged residues in SV40 might cause electrostatic repulsion between the viral particles that would destabilize its structural integrity. Furthermore, displaying positive charges on the viral surface within the hydrophobic ER lipid bilayer creates a highly energetically unfavorable condition. Thus stabilization might reflect a rather passive process in which EMC1 simply shields these charges.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of stabilization.

claims.claim: EMC1-dependent stabilization may be an active process involving recruitment of EMC1's luminal domain to provide VP1 inter-pentamer interactions.
claims.source: Alternatively, EMC1-dependent stabilization may be a more complex active process. For instance, upon recognizing exposure of aberrant residues in membrane-embedded SV40 via EMC1's transmembrane domain, EMC1's luminal domain might subsequently be recruited to provide VP1 inter-pentamer interactions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism of stabilization.

claims.claim: In infected cells devoid of EMC1, different prematurely disassembled VP1 species, likely corresponding to single and oligomeric VP1 pentamers, are generated.
claims.source: Our sucrose sedimentation analyses revealed that in infected cells devoid of EMC1, different prematurely disassembled VP1 species, likely corresponding to single and oligomeric VP1 pentamers, are generated (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by sucrose sedimentation data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: EMC1 stabilizes inter-pentamer interactions.
claims.source: This observation suggests that EMC1 stabilizes inter-pentamer interactions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the disassembly pattern observed.

claims.claim: EMC1 may exist as oligomers that enable each EMC1 monomer to crosslink to an individual VP1 molecule belonging to different pentamers.
claims.source: To enhance VP1 inter-pentamer interactions, EMC1 may exists as oligomers that enable each EMC1 monomer to crosslink to an individual VP1 molecule belonging to different pentamers.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about how EMC1 might stabilize inter-pentamer interactions.

claims.claim: EMC1 may operate in both manners to shield exposed charges and to reinforce interactions between pentamers.
claims.source: Clearly these two possibilities do not have to be mutually exclusive – EMC1 may operate in both manners to shield the presumed exposed charges and to reinforce interactions between the pentamers.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of EMC1 action.

claims.claim: Addition of DTT and EGTA to purified SV40 generates VP1 pentamers.
claims.source: In our in vitro analyses, addition of DTT and EGTA also generated VP1 pentamers (Figure 6B), whose formation can be largely suppressed by addition of purified EMC1; DTT likely mimics viral disulfide bond reduction that occurs in the ER lumen (Inoue et al., 2015), whereas EGTA may imitate loss of Ca2+ from the membrane-embedded virus when it is exposed to the low Ca2+ in the cytosol, as previously hypothesized (Schelhaas et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citations.

claims.claim: In EMC1-depleted cells, the virus does not engage the cytosolic extraction machinery composed of the Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 complex.
claims.source: Why might stabilization of membrane-embedded SV40 by EMC1 be important for membrane transport? Our studies revealed that in EMC1-depleted cells, the virus does not engage the cytosolic extraction machinery composed of the Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105 complex (Walczak et al., 2014; Ravindran et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citations.

claims.claim: The extraction machinery cannot recognize a prematurely disassembled virus in the membrane, but a largely intact virus is required for productive interaction.
claims.source: This finding suggests that the extraction machinery cannot recognize a prematurely disassembled virus in the membrane, but that a largely intact virus is instead required for productive interaction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding experiments.

claims.claim: Once the extraction machinery recognizes membrane-inserted SV40, it has the capacity to disassemble the virus.
claims.source: Interestingly, our experiments previously suggested that once the extraction machinery recognizes the membrane-inserted SV40, it has the capacity to disassemble the virus (Ravindran et al., 2015) – we postulated that this disassembly reaction might be coupled to the extraction reaction.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Initial recognition of the viral particle by the extraction machinery requires the virus to remain relatively intact.
claims.source: Thus, while initial recognition of the viral particle by the extraction machinery requires the virus to remain relatively intact, subsequent to recognition, this machinery disassembles it.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current and previous findings.

claims.claim: In humans, the EMC is composed of 10 subunits (EMC1-EMC10).
claims.source: In humans, the EMC is composed of 10 subunits (EMC1-EMC10), with EMC1 representing the largest component (Christianson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: EMC1 is sufficient to function as a molecular chaperone.
claims.source: Because our findings demonstrate that EMC1 is sufficient to function as a molecular chaperone, whether other EMC subunits can also act in a similar role or execute completely different functions remain to be clarified.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing purified EMC1 can stabilize SV40.

claims.claim: The EMC was initially identified in yeast.
claims.source: The EMC was initially identified in yeast, although its precise function was not fully clarified (Jonikas et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: The EMC was proposed to function within ERAD.
claims.source: This complex was proposed to function within an ER quality control process called ERAD, in which misfolded ER proteins are targeted to the cytosol for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation (Ruggiano et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Different EMC subunits physically associate with other components of the ERAD machinery.
claims.source: This possibility is consistent with the finding demonstrating that different EMC subunits physically associate with other components of the ERAD machinery (Christianson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: ER-to-cytosol transport of a misfolded substrate during ERAD is highly reminiscent of the pathway SV40 experiences during its ER membrane transport.
claims.source: Strikingly, ER-to-cytosol transport of a misfolded substrate during ERAD is highly reminiscent of the pathway SV40 experiences during its ER membrane transport.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison drawn between ERAD and SV40 transport pathways.

claims.claim: The EMC supports biosynthesis of multi-pass transmembrane proteins such as the ionotropic acetylcholine receptor and rhodopsin.
claims.source: Another related ER quality control function attributed to the EMC is its ability to support biosynthesis of multi-pass transmembrane proteins, such as the ionotropic acetylcholine receptor (Richard et al., 2013) and rhodopsin (Satoh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The EMC appears to serve as a transmembrane chaperone, promoting stabilization of membrane protein folding-intermediates.
claims.source: In these cases, the EMC appears to serve as a transmembrane chaperone, promoting the stabilization of the membrane protein folding-intermediates.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies of EMC function in membrane protein biosynthesis.

claims.claim: The EMC plays a critical role during flavivirus (including Zika, Dengue, and West Nile virus) infection.
claims.source: For example, a series of recent reports suggest that the EMC plays a critical role during flavivirus (including Zika, Dengue, and West Nile virus) infection (Ma et al., 2015; Savidis et al., 2016; Marceau et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: Replication and assembly of flaviviruses are events associated with the ER membrane.
claims.source: As a wealth of literature has established that replication and assembly of flaviviruses are events in their life cycle associated with the ER membrane (Ravindran et al., 2016), it is perhaps not surprising that this ER membrane protein complex might exert a role during their infection.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: The molecular basis by which the EMC controls flavivirus infection remains completely unknown.
claims.source: However, despite these reports, the molecular basis by which the EMC controls flavivirus infection remains completely unknown.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Mutant EMC1 alleles are strongly associated with various human neurodevelopmental disorders, including global developmental delay and cerebellar atrophy.
claims.source: Finally, mutant EMC1 alleles were recently found to be strongly associated with various human neurodevelopmental disorders, including global developmental delay and cerebellar atrophy (Harel et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

results.result: EMC1 is identified as a binding partner of the ER membrane J-protein C18. Mass spectrometry and immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate that C18 preferentially binds to EMC1 compared to other J-proteins (B14 and B12), and this interaction is observed in multiple cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C40 are well-supported by complementary experimental approaches including mass spectrometry (Figure 1A, Table 1), immunoblotting validation (Figure 1B), and affinity purification in multiple cell types (Figures 1C-D). The preferential binding of C18 to EMC1 over other J-proteins is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: EMC1 promotes SV40 and BK polyomavirus infection. siRNA-mediated depletion of EMC1 significantly impairs infection by both SV40 and the human BK PyV, demonstrating a broad role in polyomavirus infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C43-C45 are supported by infection assays (Figure 2C) showing statistically significant reduction in viral infection upon EMC1 knockdown. Controls demonstrate specificity (no ER stress induction, no effect on other ER membrane proteins). The conclusion of broad importance (C45) is justified by effects on both viruses.

results.result: EMC1 specifically promotes SV40 ER-to-cytosol membrane transport without affecting viral trafficking to the ER or other ER transport processes. EMC1 depletion blocks cytosol arrival of SV40 but does not affect ER arrival or cholera toxin transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51, C54 are supported by cell fractionation assays (Figures 3A-E) demonstrating reduced cytosolic SV40 in EMC1-depleted cells while ER-localized virus levels remain unchanged. The negative control with cholera toxin (C51) strengthens the specificity argument. The conclusion of specific function (C50, C54) is well-justified.

results.result: The conserved transmembrane residue D961 of EMC1 is critical for SV40 infection. D961A mutant EMC1 fails to rescue infection in knockdown cells, while T976A mutant does rescue. The D961A mutant is properly localized, oriented, and can bind C18 and EMC3, indicating the defect is specific to viral function.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C70 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: sequence conservation (Figure 4A), localization studies (Figure 4B), deglycosylation assays (Figure 4C), binding assays (Figures 4D, 4F), and critically, knockdown-rescue experiments (Figures 4E, 4G). The specificity of D961's role is demonstrated by proper localization and binding of the mutant to cellular partners but failure to rescue infection.

results.result: EMC1 binds to SV40 during infection at the time of ER membrane penetration (~7 hpi) in a D961-dependent manner. The interaction is salt-sensitive, suggesting electrostatic binding. The D961A mutant and truncated EMC1 show reduced virus binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are supported by time-course immunoprecipitation (Figure 5A), mutant binding studies (Figures 5B-C), and salt sensitivity experiments (Figure 5D). The temporal correlation with membrane penetration (C73) is an inference but reasonable given prior knowledge (C71). The correlation between binding and infection (C78) is well-established across multiple experiments.

results.result: EMC1 directly interacts with partially destabilized SV40 in vitro. Purified EMC1 binds to DTT/EGTA-treated SV40 but not native virus, and this interaction requires D961. VP2/VP3 contribute to the interaction along with VP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by in vitro binding assays with purified components (Figures 5E-H). The differential binding to treated vs. untreated virus (C82-C83) demonstrates specificity for destabilized virus. The D961 requirement (C84) is consistent with cell-based data. The VP2/VP3 contribution (C85) is demonstrated by reduced binding to VP1-VLP.

results.result: EMC1 stabilizes ER-localized SV40 and prevents premature viral disassembly. In EMC1-depleted cells, a portion of ER-localized SV40 disassembles prematurely into VP1 pentamers, and the virus becomes more sensitive to proteolytic digestion. This is specific to EMC1 depletion and not a general consequence of blocking ER transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 are supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation (Figure 6A) and limited proteolysis (Figure 6B) assays. The appearance of disassembled virus in EMC1-depleted but not SGTA- or C18-depleted cells (C88) demonstrates specificity. The two independent assays provide converging evidence for the stabilization function.

results.result: EMC1 protects SV40 against DTT/EGTA-induced disassembly in vitro in a D961-dependent manner. WT EMC1 protects >66% of virus while D961A mutant protects only ~18%. Protection requires EMC1 to be present during destabilization, not added afterward.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by in vitro reconstitution experiments (Figures 6C-D) with purified components. The quantification (C95) provides clear evidence of D961's importance. The requirement for simultaneous incubation (C93) suggests a co-stabilization mechanism. These in vitro results strongly support the cell-based findings.

results.result: EMC1 is required for SV40 to engage the cytosolic extraction machinery (Hsc70-SGTA-Hsp105). In EMC1-depleted cells, SV40 cannot bind to Hsc70 or SGTA, but the extraction machinery remains properly tethered to ER J-proteins. This suggests premature disassembly prevents recognition by the extraction machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are supported by affinity purification experiments (Figures 7A-B) showing loss of virus binding to extraction machinery components but preservation of machinery-J-protein interactions. The inference that premature disassembly prevents recognition (C102) is logical given the disassembly data from Figure 6.

results.result: EMC1 acts as a molecular chaperone, using its D961 transmembrane residue to bind and stabilize membrane-embedded partially destabilized SV40, preventing premature disassembly and maintaining the virus in a transport-competent state for extraction machinery engagement.
results.evaluation: This integrative conclusion (C4-C6, C9, C105-C106, C108) is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence: D961-dependent binding to destabilized virus, prevention of premature disassembly, protection against DTT/EGTA-induced disassembly, and requirement for extraction machinery engagement. The chaperone designation is appropriate given the stabilization function.

results.result: Coordinated destabilization-stabilization drives membrane transport of non-enveloped viruses. This represents a novel principle where opposing forces work together to achieve successful membrane penetration.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C109, C111 represent the main conceptual advance of the paper. This conclusion is supported by the demonstration that both destabilization (prior work cited) and stabilization (current work) are required for successful membrane transport. The novelty is justified as this coordinated mechanism has not been previously described for non-enveloped viruses.

results.result: EMC1 depletion by siRNA is specific and does not cause off-target effects. Knockdown does not affect levels of other ER membrane proteins (B14, B12, C18, BAP31, Derlin-1) or induce ER stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 2A) and XBP1 splicing assays (Figure 2B). These controls are essential for validating the specificity of subsequent phenotypes and are appropriately executed.

results.result: Knocking down other EMC subunits variably attenuates SV40 infection, suggesting some may have roles in viral ER membrane penetration with different levels of impact.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by knockdown and infection data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). However, C47 is appropriately cautious as speculation. This result suggests complexity in EMC function but requires further investigation to define specific roles of other subunits.

results.result: SV40 triggers EMC1 mobilization into BAP31-positive foci structures, while the control ER membrane protein Sel1L does not mobilize into these structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This provides additional evidence for EMC1's specific involvement in SV40 membrane penetration and is consistent with prior observations for other factors involved in this process.

results.result: EMC1's predicted structural organization includes a signal sequence (aa 1-21), luminal domain (aa 22-958), membrane domain (aa 959-979), and cytosolic domain (aa 980-993).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are based on computational prediction rather than experimental determination. While the predictions are reasonable for a type I transmembrane protein, they have not been experimentally validated in this study. The deglycosylation and localization data provide some support but do not definitively confirm the boundaries.

results.result: Purified WT and D961A EMC1 samples do not contain other EMC subunits as determined by mass spectrometry.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is stated to be supported by mass spectrometry analysis, though the data are not shown. This is an important control for the in vitro experiments demonstrating that EMC1 alone is sufficient for the stabilization function.

results.result: EMC1's interaction stabilizes the overall SV40 architecture within the ER lipid bilayer or at the earliest phase of membrane insertion.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 is explicitly presented as speculation in the Discussion. While consistent with the experimental data, the precise location and timing of EMC1's stabilization function (within bilayer vs. at membrane border) has not been experimentally determined. This represents a mechanistic hypothesis requiring further investigation.

results.result: EMC1 may recognize positively-charged residues exposed in membrane-inserted SV40 via its D961 residue, with the transmembrane domain functioning as a 'sensor' for aberrant membrane-spanning residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C113, C115, C117 are explicitly presented as speculation in the Discussion. While the electrostatic interaction model is consistent with D961's negative charge and salt sensitivity of binding, direct evidence for positively-charged residues on SV40 being the binding site is lacking. This represents a reasonable mechanistic hypothesis requiring experimental validation.

results.result: EMC1 stabilization may occur through passive charge shielding, active recruitment of the luminal domain for inter-pentamer interactions, or both mechanisms. EMC1 may exist as oligomers to crosslink VP1 molecules from different pentamers.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119, C122-C123 are explicitly presented as speculation about mechanism. While the disassembly pattern (C120-C121) suggests inter-pentamer stabilization, the specific molecular mechanism (passive vs. active, monomeric vs. oligomeric) has not been experimentally determined. These represent testable hypotheses for future work.

results.result: Background information on polyomaviruses, SV40 structure, trafficking, and the established role of destabilization in membrane transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C31 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide essential context for the current work and are accurately presented based on the citations provided.

results.result: Background information on the ER membrane protein complex (EMC), its composition, and previously described functions in ERAD and membrane protein biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36, C129, C131-C136 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide context for why EMC1 was investigated and are accurately presented.

results.result: Prior knowledge about SV40 ER membrane penetration timing, partial destabilization in the ER, and exposure of VP2/VP3 in membrane-inserted virus. DTT/EGTA treatment mimics ER-induced conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C80-C81, C114, C124 represent prior knowledge from the authors' previous work and other studies, appropriately cited. The DTT/EGTA treatment as a mimic of ER conditions is well-established and validated by the current results.

results.result: Broader context: coordinated destabilization-stabilization in HIV entry, EMC's role in flavivirus infection, and association of EMC1 mutations with neurodevelopmental disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C110, C138-C141 represent established knowledge from recent literature, appropriately cited. These provide broader context for the significance of the findings beyond polyomavirus biology.

results.result: The extraction machinery cannot recognize prematurely disassembled virus but requires largely intact virus for productive interaction. Once recognized, the machinery can disassemble the virus during extraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 integrate current findings (C125-C126) with prior work (C127). The inference that intact virus is required for recognition (C126) is well-supported by the binding data. The model of recognition followed by disassembly (C128) is consistent with prior work cited.

results.result: EMC1 is sufficient to function as a molecular chaperone based on in vitro experiments with purified EMC1.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is supported by the in vitro reconstitution experiments (Figures 5E-G, 6C-D) showing purified EMC1 can bind and stabilize SV40. The mass spectrometry confirmation that other EMC subunits are absent (C79) strengthens this conclusion of sufficiency.

results.result: Virus stabilization can serve a crucial function during viral entry, contrasting with the typical role of host-encoded stabilization forces in viral assembly.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 represents a conceptual advance supported by the current work. The contrast with viral assembly (cited prior work) is accurate, and the demonstration of stabilization during entry is novel for non-enveloped viruses.

results.result: VP1-VLP lacking VP2 and VP3 displays less efficient binding to EMC1 compared to WT SV40.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by experimental data in Figure 5H showing reduced binding of VP1-VLP to EMC1. This supports the conclusion that VP2/VP3 contribute to the interaction (C85).

results.result: In EMC1-depleted cells, different prematurely disassembled VP1 species are generated, suggesting EMC1 stabilizes inter-pentamer interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by sucrose sedimentation data (Figure 6A) showing multiple disassembled species. The inference about inter-pentamer stabilization (C121) is reasonable based on the disassembly pattern, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.
